meta.source: Air-Conditioning, Heating and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI), Water Heater Calculator: Worksheet for Estimating Peak Hour Demand/First Hour Rating (2011)
meta.notes: AHRI runs the certification program for water heater ratings, and DOE's Building America Solution Center (PNNL) describes this AHRI method as the industry standard for sizing storage water heaters. The worksheet assumes no water conservation measures, which suits sizing because a heater lasts more than a decade. Rule: choose a first hour rating (FHR) at least equal to the peak hour demand. DOE's own Energy Saver worksheet (removed from energy.gov in 2026; archived 2017 copy) used smaller per-use values; they are kept below for comparison only.

fhrRule.source: Select a storage water heater with a first-hour rating equal to or greater than the peak hour demand (PNNL Building America Solution Center, DHW First Hour Rating tool, based on AHRI guidance)

doeArchived2017.source: DOE Energy Saver, Sizing a New Water Heater, worksheet (archived January 27, 2017; adapted from the FEMP Energy Cost Calculator)

householdPresets.source: Hot Water Math editorial assumption: a typical busiest hour for each household size, chosen so the peak-hour demand lands inside American Water Heater's first hour rating range for the same family size (data/household-size-guides.json). Change the counts to match your own busiest hour.

margin.source: Hot Water Math editorial assumption: optional 10% margin for homes that often run several uses at once. A. O. Smith advises a first hour rating that equals or slightly exceeds peak-hour demand.

largeTub.source: Rheem, How to size a water heater: "While small tubs are usually about 40 gallons, deep soaking tubs can hold up to 140 gallons" and "most people bathe at temperatures between 102°F to 106°F" (checked 2026-11-14). The size calculator turns a tub fill (gallons) into hot water with the tank share of the mix: fill × (104 − inlet) ÷ (setpoint − inlet), at the 120 °F setpoint and the DOE test inlet (58 °F). AHRI's 20 gallons per bath stays the value for a standard tub.

showerFlow.source: Hot Water Math assumption: AHRI's 20 gallons per shower is read as a 2.5 GPM shower head (the federal maximum; the worksheet "assumes no water conservation measures"), so a custom shower head flow scales it: 20 × your GPM ÷ 2.5.
